kūrca
------------------------------------------
Kuśa grass (Poa cynosuroides) is widely used in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् for various purposes.
Kūrca is a bundle of this grass generally used as a seat, a sort of a cushion, on which the sacrificer and the अध्वर्यु priest sit.
Kūrca is also the name of a small elongated plate made of कुश grass or Vāraṇa wood (Crataeva roxburghii) about 36 aṅgulas in length and shaped like a tortoise or a dolphin. It is kept on the west of the आहवनीय fire. The śrucas (sacrificial ladles) are kept on it when not in use.

Kūrma
(‘the tortoise’)
------------------------------------------
On the suggestion of Mahāviṣṇu, the देवस् (gods) and the दानवस् (demons) started churning the क्षीरसमुद्र (the ocean of milk) for obtaining अमृत or ambrosia. The mount मेरु was the churning rod and वासुकि, the serpent king was the rope. During the process of churning, the mount मेरु started sinking. So, at the request of the two parties, Mahāviṣṇu took the form of a huge कूर्म or tortoise and supported the मेरु mountain on his back. This is considered as the Kūrmāvatāra or कूर्म इन्चर्नतिओन् of Mahāviṣṇu.
Iconographically he is shown either as a tortoise or with the lower part as a tortoise and the upper part in the human form but with four hands, two hands carrying the emblems of विष्णु (śaṅkha or conch and चक्र or the discus) and the other two showing the poses of abhaya (protection from fear) and varada (giving of boons). Sometimes the गदा (mace) is shown in the right hand instead of the discus.
Kūrma is also the name of one of the five upaprāṇas (minor vital-airs) responsible for opening the eyelids.
Kūrma is also the name of a मुद्रा (handpose) used in पूजा or worship.

Kurukṣetra
------------------------------------------
Though कुरुक्षेत्र has been closely associated with the fratricidal war of the Mahābhārata, it has also been hailed as the ‘dharmakṣetra’ (field of righteousness) (vide Bhagavadgītā 1.1). It is almost the same as the modern कुरुक्षेत्र, 40 kms. (25 miles) to the east of Ambala in the Haryana State.
There is no doubt that it was consi-dered a very sacred spot even from the most ancient times. It was the place where the gods had performed many yāgas or sacrifices. It was the heart of Vedic culture in the olden days. The lands to the southern and the northern parts were known as Khāṇḍava and Tūrghna. There was also a desert near it.
According to another version it was the sacrificial ground of the king कुरु, the son of Saṁvaraṇa and Tapatī, of the चन्द्रवṁश.
It has been known by several other names such as Brahmāvarta, Kurujāṅgala (situated between the rivers सरस्वती and Dṛṣadvatī), Brahmasaras, Rāmahrada, समन्तपञ्चक, विनशन and so on.
The lake in कुरुक्षेत्र was originally five big pools of blood of the kṣattriyas killed by परशुराम which was converted into a single lake of holy water by the grace of his पितृस् or forefathers who were pleased by his penance and forgave him. It is oblong in shape and is 1063 metres (3546 ft.) in length. On the days of solar एच्लिप्से, lakhs of people gather here for a holy dip.
The forests mentioned in the Mahābhārata like the Kāmyakavana, Aditivana and Vyāsavana were near कुरुक्षेत्र.
Hastināpura (situated at a distance of 104 kms. or 65 miles to the north-west of Delhi), इन्द्रप्रस्थ (now a part of old Delhi), Sthāṇeśvara (the present Thanesar in Haryana) and Pṛthūdaka (the present Pehova) were the famous cities of कुरु-क्षेत्र. कुरुक्षेत्र has been considered a very holy place for the performance of śrāddhas.
Varāhatīrtha (where विष्णु stood in his इन्चर्नतिओन् as a boar), व्यासतीर्थ (where व्यास wanted to give up his body, but was dissuaded from doing so) and Saptasarasvata (where शिव appeared before the sage Maṅkaṇaka) are the holy spots near कुरुक्षेत्र apart from the place where the Bhagavadgītā was taught by कृष्ण to अर्जुन.
The modern regions of Karnal, Panipat, Sonepat and Amin roughly correspond to the ancient कुरुक्षेत्र.
After independence, कुरुक्षेत्र has been developed as a big pilgrim and tourist centre.

Kuru
------------------------------------------
The words Kurujāṅgala, कुरु-pāñcāla and कुरुक्षेत्र are often found in the Hindu epics and the पुराणस्. All these are connected with कुरु, who was the founder of the dynasty Kuruvaṁśa. He was the son of Saṁvaraṇa (of चन्द्रवṁश or the race of the मोओन्) and Tapatī.
There was another कुरु, the seventh son of the king आग्नीध्र who had nine sons. He became the ruler of 1/9 th of his ड़थेर्’s kingdom which came to be known as Kuruvarṣa.
Kuru, the son of the king Saṁvaraṇa, built a yāgaśālā (a huge campus for performing वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्) between the river सरस्वती and Dṛśadvatī, later known as कुरुक्षेत्र. There is no unanimity among the scholars about this कुरुक्षेत्र being the same where the महाभारत war took place.

-1161)
------------------------------------------
Great spiritual teachers often have great disciples to carry on their work even after they leave this world. One such disciple of Rāmānuja (A.
-1137), considered as his ‘jñānaputra’, (spiritual son) was कुरुकेश, also known as Tirukkurugaippirān Piḷḷān. He was the son of Rāmānuja’s maternal uncle Śrīśailapūrṇa and was born in Tirumalai in A.
. Rāmānuja chose him to complete one of the three promises he had made to fulfil the last wishes of Yāmunā-cārya (A.

-1042). This was to get composed an authoritative commentary in Tamil on the Tiruvāymoḷi of Nammāḷvar.
He had acquired great erudition in the Sanskrit and the Tamil scriptures. Equally laudable was his single-minded devotion to Rāmānuja.
When Rāmānuja got an image of लक्ष्मी-हयग्रीव (an aspect of विष्णु) in Kashmir, he gave it to कुरुकेश for worship and reverential maintenance.
He was the first successor of Rāmānuja as the आचार्य (pontiff).
He wrote a detailed commentary in the मणिप्रवाऌअ language (Sanskritised Tamil) on the Tiruvāymoḷi of Nammāḷvar in 6000 stanzas (called ‘granthas’). This work is known as Ārāyirappaḍi. It is said to contain all the important doctrinal points expounded in the Śrībhāṣya of Rāmānuja.
He was also a good speaker in Sanskrit as well as Tamil, and conducted discourses throughout his life.
He passed away in A.

Kūreśa
------------------------------------------
Great religious leaders have often been helped by highly dedicated disciples who assisted them tirelessly but, themselves remained in the background. कूरेश a trusted disciple of Rāmānuja (A.

-1137) was one such fortunate सोउल्. He was a wealthy land-lord living near Kāñcī-puram (in Tamil Nadu). He was as gener-ous as he was rich. His wife, Āṇḍāḷamma too, was of the same disposition.
The couple renounced everything and followed Rāmānuja wherever he went. When they stayed at श्रीरङ्गम्, कूरेश used to live by begging. One day, a divinely handsome boy appeared before Āṇḍāḷamma and gave her the sacred ड़ोओद् offerings of Śrī रङ्गनाथ, the main deity of the temple there. After consuming this sacramental ड़ोओद्, she conceived and gave birth to twins. Rāmānuja named them as पराशर and व्यास.
Parāśara later became a great scholar and wrote an erudite commentary on the famous hymn, the Viṣṇusahasranāma.
When the Coḷa king Kulottuṅga, who was a fanatic Śaiva, wanted to eliminate Rāmānuja and sent his men, कूरेश impersonated himself as Rāmānuja and went to his court. The evil king gouged out his eyes! Thus कूरेश sacrificed himself to save his गुरु.
He spent his last days near मदुरै.
See also RĀMĀNUJA.
